$NVDA $MU $SNDK $LITE THE COMEBACK CAMPAIGN AND THE VETO

WHAT IS REPORTED

The Financial Times, citing multiple people familiar with the matter, reports that Jensen Huang is discussing a comeback as Nvidia chief executive with his allies, days after the board accepted his resignation. A war room of Silicon Valley executives is being put together to lobby for his return.

This did not start today. On November 13, Altimeter and Atreides wrote to the board urging a slow, measured, and deliberate approach to the leadership question, expressly including the potential return of Jensen Huang. A petition to reinstate him is circulating, with public signatories. The rehabilitation narrative made its public debut on a flagship podcast on November 14. Today the campaign got its first prestige-press carriage.

The market's first vote was a spike. Nvidia perpetuals jumped about 2.7 percent on the headlines, touching 165.92 before settling near 164.

THE COUNTERWEIGHT, IN THE SAME NEWS CYCLE

On Sunday morning television, the Treasury Secretary said Nvidia needs a dramatic shakeup in leadership and should go outside the company to find it. In the same hours, Congress moved to tighten export rules on AI chips after the scandal, and the company was ordered to explain a reported 12 billion dollars of chip supply to China.

That is the terrain the comeback campaign has to cross. It does not merely have to persuade ten directors. It has to beat the stated position of the administration, on the record, on a Sunday show, while congressional chairs are conditioning the company's future on leadership that makes national security the top priority.

WHY THE RETURN STILL DOES NOT WORK

The admitted facts cannot be un-admitted. Two relationships with subordinates, one of them a direct report. Written assurances to his own general counsel that the interactions were standard business dealings. The November 8 admission. The board's acceptance of the resignation on November 11. A securities class action already filed. Insurers who have already priced the conduct. A public search process, an interim chief executive already holding staff meetings, and December hearings already on the calendar.

A board that reinstates him owns every line of that, in front of the plaintiffs, the auditors, the insurers, and the committees. Huang holds roughly 3 to 4 percent of the vote and no control mechanism. There is no lever that forces this outcome, only persuasion, and persuasion runs into the Treasury Secretary's veto.

WHAT THE CAMPAIGN IS ACTUALLY FOR

Shaping the landing. The successor choice, the severance and clawback terms, the emeritus shape of the exit, and the historical record are all still unwritten, and a live comeback story is leverage on every one of them. The letter's real audience was never the vote count. It was the terms.

WHAT WOULD CHANGE THIS READ

• The search pausing or going quiet
• Board silence extending past the earnings print and the December hearings
• A filing that softens the November record

None of the three is present.

THE TRADE

Tuesday's print is now a governance event as well as a numbers event. The comeback headlines bid the stock because they promise the old regime's certainty. The investment case for holding through the print never depended on who sits in the chief executive's chair, and neither does the restructuring that follows it. What the campaign changes is the noise around the print, not the bogeys: the guide, the tone, and the tripwires are exactly where they were.

我最新的產業調查與研究結論：

1. 訂單能見度與出貨規劃：
受惠於 OpenAI 與 Anthropic 強勁新訂單，Google TPU 出貨能見度已達 2029 年，優於 Nvidia GPU 與其他 AI ASIC（多數為 4Q27–2Q28）。

(1) 自 2028 年起，v9 將成 Google 自建算力的主力方案，v8 系列（8t／8i 或其設計變種）訂單可視為來自 OpenAI 與 Anthropic。

(2) 2028–2029 年合計需求數量：OpenAI 約 12M（聯發科設計的 8t），Anthropic 約 14M（Broadcom 設計的 8i），兩者需求均呈逐年成長趨勢。OpenAI 採買斷，Anthropic 則是租賃與買斷都有。

(3) 考量供應鏈限制，2027–2029 年較合理的 TPU 出貨估算分別為 8–9M、14–15M、16–18M。市場普遍預期 AI 資本支出於 2028 年見頂，但此規劃顯示 TPU 在 2029 年仍具出貨成長動能，關鍵在於 AI 服務龍頭 OpenAI 與 Anthropic 的直接訂單。

🚨 THE “OVERHEAD SUPPLY WALL” ABOVE SPY IS PROBABLY NOT A WALL.

Nearly half of SPY’s volume since July traded between 761 and 773.

SPY closed Friday at 754.37.

The busiest price was 767, leaving a massive block of supposedly trapped investors above the market.

The conventional argument is simple:

Those investors will sell when SPY returns to breakeven, creating resistance and capping any rally.

It sounds logical.

The data does not support it.

We preregistered the test, built point-in-time volume profiles and studied SPY, QQQ, IWM and DIA back to 2016.

If overhead supply actually suppresses price, larger overhead volume should predict less upside.

It predicted the opposite.

Across the four index ETFs, heavier overhead supply was associated with greater 10-session upside, not less.

The result remained positive across 20, 60 and 120-session volume profiles and in both halves of the sample.

Then we isolated 24 comparable SPY setups.

Over the following 20 sessions:

Average return: +1.80%

Median return: +3.17%

Positive outcomes: 67%

Reached the overhead volume shelf: 67%

But here is the important part.

Comparable SPY pullbacks reached any price the same distance above the market roughly 76% of the time.

The volume shelf was not a special magnet.

It was not a reliable ceiling either.

It was simply another price.

This is not a buy signal. The sample is small, and the outcomes varied widely.

It is the removal of a sell signal.

The current 767 shelf is only 1.7% above SPY. Historically, SPY reaches a level that close within 20 sessions roughly three-quarters of the time.

Do not automatically fade 767 because a volume profile labels it “overhead supply.”

In index ETFs, volume does not tell you who is trapped, who is hedged or who still needs to sell.

The wall is a compelling story pasted onto a histogram.

The evidence says SPY can trade straight through it.

I’m struggling with the line of thought that says Jensen should be brought back or that his exit was unjustified. Several things at play here:

1/ Personal indiscretions. I grant fully that these are irrelevant as a general matter. 

2/ Indiscretions with subordinates. I can even get behind the idea that Jensen is a uniquely special circumstance and we should overlook it. 

3/ Indiscretions with a potential Chinese intel asset. Let’s also fully believe the recent reporting that suggests the evidence is suspect. 

4/ Jensen as the last defense against misguided export control policy and closed lab hegemony. This is where things get tricky. But even so, let’s grant that this is a potentially existentially important counter-competitive role to play and almost no one else has the stature to do it. 

5/ At worst, he had knowledge of hardware diversion to China in violation of export controls. This is where it becomes an incredibly easy decision. Regardless of what you believe about the controls (and I believe they are both against US interests and even worse, ineffective), knowingly circumventing them is an egregious violation of shareholder and public trust. It’s also illegal. 

6/ At best, he created the perception in his affair with Alice that he was vulnerable to influence by questionable partners that could be diverting hardware to China. He can’t really change this fact regardless how true the rest of it is. It’s deeply negligent and a failure of judgment. 

7/ By lying about it initially, he put in motion a series of actions by his company that at least created the perception they were interfering in a federal probe or covering something up. It put an enormous company at risk of legal, financial, and even personal liability. 

1-4 are forgivable. Any combination of 5-7 is pretty easy IMO. An investigation can come up roses in a technical sense, but the conflicts and risk exposure along the way, ones that Nvidia will be dealing with for a long time with or without him, won’t ever really change.

Big week on 20VC with @HarryStebbings and @rodriscoll. 

Sequoia closed London and killed Scouts and Arc, Jensen resigned the day after we recorded, Anthropic's IPO book is reportedly 6x oversubscribed, and agents kept eating seat-based B2B.

My takes:

#1. The biggest Sequoia news wasn't London. It was winding down the evergreen fund. 

Holding generational assets for decades was the best idea in venture. It launched right before stocks fell 30%, and LPs don't want to be forced to hold.

#2. Sequoia can cover Europe from the Bay above pre-seed

The best European founders are already here every month. Mati from ElevenLabs is at every dinner I go to. Pre-seed still needs someone local doing the hands-on work.

#3. On Tuesday I said Jensen needed a pass. Rory said you can hope for a pass but can't assume one. Rory was right. 

He resigned Wednesday, and the CFO is now interim CEO. China comes out the biggest loser here. Selling GPUs there, or parking them just over the border, just got a lot harder.

#4. The AI trade doesn't crack on supply

Not on data centers, not on AMD taking share. It cracks only if demand cracks, and you'll see that in OpenAI and Anthropic ARR first. The $2.5T NASDAQ drop was hedge fund pods getting stopped out.

#5. I called Anthropic's IPO fatigued. A 6x book says otherwise

The $70 to $78 range isn't the price. It could still go up before pricing on Nov 18. Either way, you'd rather be Anthropic than OpenAI right now: public, with the float and roughly $200B in cash.

#6. OpenAI reaccelerated to 70% annualized revenue growth in Q3, and enterprise is now the majority of revenue

It's a two-horse race, and the next question is how price-sensitive token demand is. If you cut price 20% and usage goes up 21%, revenue grows. If usage goes up 15%, it shrinks.

#7. IC this week was Zipline at $21.5B, fal at $16B and Revolut at $115B. I'd do all three. 

If I have to pick, it's fal. Sometimes in venture you have to be a tourist and ride the wave. Harry and Rory both took Revolut, which is set up to become Europe's biggest bank.

#8. Stolen AI API keys are the crime of the yea

Bot swarms are hitting everyone, and my own Claude limit had defaulted to $100K. It's better than stealing Rolexes off wrists in London. And customers can't leave their inference provider, because there's nowhere else with the capacity.

#9. Dialpad buying Ada for about $430M in stock isn't an exit

What depresses me more is that so many pre-AI companies still ship at 2021 speed. If your 2027 plan is "build an AI-native team next year," that was the 2025 plan.

#10. Cloudflare grew 39% on agents while Atlassian fell on seat growth

Agents don't care about your UX. If it's not an agentic beneficiary, I don't want to hear about it. Figma below $10B is the cautionary tale: turn down $20B, execute brilliantly for three years, and you can still end up worth half.

Rory's best line: "You could work for the next three years, do an amazing job, grow your damn company 40% a year, get the damn thing public. And at the end of that, you're going to be worth half what you are today. No one ever said capitalism was fair or easy."

As ridiculous as this sounds, yes, it looks like Tesla is rushing this out just to win a bet against a YouTuber. Absolutely insane behavior. We've seen this movie before. In June 2025, Tesla did a single "autonomous delivery" of a Model Y to meet a Musk deadline, then never did it again.

Tesla always pitched the Cybercab as a vehicle for its Robotaxi network. Now, seven weeks before the deadline, a personal-use version shows up that's invite-only, Texas-only, banned from doing the one thing it was designed for, and attached to a subscription Musk himself says is too expensive. If you set out to build a product whose main job was letting Musk claim he won a Twitter bet, it would look a lot like this.

This Cybercab offering is completely broken. The value proposition is awful. As others have put it, it's a permanent variable-rate lease starting at $300 a month, with a ridiculous $30,000 down payment.

What do you get for this deal? A 2-seater vehicle that only works in small, incomplete, geo-fenced areas and has no steering wheel to do anything else with it. Meanwhile, Tesla insists that the Model Y, like the ones used in its current Robotaxi service alongside the Cybercab, uses the same self-driving technology.

You can buy one for $40,000, and you get a lot more car than the Cybercab; then you can pay $99 a month for FSD instead of $300 a month and that works everywhere with supervision. Tesla is supposed to let current Tesla owners drive without supervision in the same geo-fenced areas, which would basically be the same product as what Tesla is offering right now with the Cybertruck, but you are not a slave to Tesla, which can brick your car at any time or change the terms. Model Y has a steering wheel.

This offer simply makes no sense, and Musk is sort of admitting it by saying the price should be the same as FSD, not $300 a month.

Bitcoin fell 19% into the biggest IPO ever. Now it's down 18% heading into the second biggest.

SpaceX raised $75B when it went public on June 12. In the 50 days before it listed, Bitcoin dropped 19%. Anthropic plans to raise up to $64B when it lists next week, and Bitcoin is down 18% over the same stretch. Overlay the two and they look almost the same.

What happened after the SpaceX IPO is the notable part. Bitcoin bottomed 18 days after the listing, then recovered all the way. By Day 100, it was above where it started.

Bitcoin around the SpaceX IPO:

Day -50 to IPO day: -19%
Low (Day +18): -25%
Day +50: still -20%
Around Day +70: a sharp rally
Day +100: +3.7%

From the IPO-day close to Day +100, Bitcoin gained 28%. From the low, it gained 39%.

The takeaway is that the selling came in the run-up to the listing. The bottom had effectively happened by the IPO, and the recovery came relatively shortly after, and it came all at once.

If Anthropic follows the same pattern, most of the drawdown is behind us, and it could reverse quickly over the next couple of months. And Bitcoin is sitting right at its 200-week moving average.

Map the SpaceX path onto today's price and you get roughly $90k by late February. Markets rarely follow a comparison like this exactly. But we remain very constructive on both the technicals and the fundamentals heading into 2027, and it's not hard to imagine what the narrative would be if anything close to this plays out.

Ate at Benihana on weekend. Been reading up on it and super interesting. Does 20%+ operating margins. Great for restaurants. 

Harvard Business School even did a case study on benefits of hibachi/teppanyaki model:

▫️MAXIMIZE REAL ESTATE: Back kitchen area mostly for prep. Leaves more space for seating in dining area. Grill tables standardized to seat 8.  Don’t have to deal with a bunch of different seating set ups.

▫️EFFICIENT TABLE SERVICE: Table service typically begins once 8 people seated. Chefs master the same sequence: rice, vegetables, protein, jokes (and that glorious volcano onion). Less chance of mistakes and table times predictable. 

When chef is done, leaves grill table, a subtle hint for guests to leave (and turn the table for more customers).

A table having to wait to seat 8 before cooking does introduce inefficiencies, though…but, during this time, customers usually asked to hang out at the bar (which sells high margin sushi and drinks).

▫️MENU SIMPLIFICATION: Majority of grill menu is three proteins (chicken, steak, shrimp), vegetables (zucchini, onions), rice and sauces. 

The menu mixes and matches options (I had Rocky’s favourite: steak & chicken) to look like variety, but it’s really only handful of ingredients.

Benihana can buy these ingredients in bulk to save. There’s less wasted food and easier for chef to memorize/master cooking (straightforwardness of menu also makes it easier for chef to entertain — eg. egg shell in hat — and drop them jokes).

🚨 64,000 BITCOIN MINERS HIJACKED IN MASSIVE ATTACK

An estimated 64,000 Bitcoin miners representing 13 EH/s of hashrate were reportedly hijacked overnight, with their mining power redirected to OCEAN mining pool and payouts assigned to an attacker-controlled Bitcoin address.

The attack reportedly began around 8 PM CT on November 14.

OCEAN’s dashboard shows a sharp spike in hashrate, briefly approaching 50 EH/s before falling back toward 40 EH/s.

CoreX Hosting first raised the alarm, reporting that miners were being redirected without authorization.

One affected operator says their entire mining farm was hijacked and identified Luxor’s Commander mining management software as the source of the compromise.

Other operators reported similar unauthorized pool changes several days earlier, potentially pointing to a broader incident.

CoreX later reported that the attack appeared to be over, with the hijacked hashrate falling from 13 EH/s to approximately 100 PH/s.

The attackers reportedly failed to mine a Bitcoin block during the hijack, meaning no block rewards were collected.

posts.name: James E. Thorne
posts.text:
The Oil Glut Is Coming Before the Futures Market Sees It

The Federal Reserve is fighting the last war. It raised rates into an oil shock that is now reversing on its own. Futures still show a market short of crude, but the physical market says otherwise, and it usually moves first.

Start on the US Gulf Coast. Western Canada Select trades $26 a barrel below WTI, against a 20-year average of $17. In Houston last month the discount hit a record $23. Heavy-crude refiners are full, Venezuelan barrels are back and costly freight has made re-exporting the surplus uneconomic. Markets do not discount barrels they need.

The signs are spreading. The International Energy Agency reports supply exceeding demand for the first time since the Iran war began. Inventories rose 52m barrels in October and oil at sea hit 2bn barrels. Dated Brent trades below its futures contract, and Brent’s one-month spread has narrowed from $3.87 to $2.71 in two weeks.

Freight agrees: Gulf-to-China supertanker rates are down almost a quarter from October’s record, and Atlantic rates are back below prewar levels.

All this with Iran exporting nothing. Iraq is pumping at a seven-year high, Saudi output is near prewar and Brent is 30 per cent off its peak. The world can live without Iranian oil; Tehran cannot live without selling it.

Now take Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent at his word. He says Hormuz flows are back to pre-conflict levels, minus Iran. The IEA’s surplus assumes Gulf exports remain 26 per cent below prewar. If Bessent is right, that gap is already closing, and each barrel it closes lands in a market already oversupplied. The glut would be bigger, and arrive sooner, than forecasters expect.

That is the Gulf’s real problem. Asian refiners have learnt to buy elsewhere: record Canadian barrels via Trans Mountain, plus more from the US, Guyana and Brazil. Wartime contracts outlast wars.

Riyadh met such challenges in 1986, 2014 and 2020 with volume, and prices halved in 2014; watch OPEC+ on 29 November.

Nor is services inflation a reason to hold firm. Services CPI has been above 2 per cent 94 per cent of the time over the past 60 years. That is its normal state, not a new threat.

For investors, the energy war premium is a sell. For central banks, the lesson is older: supply shocks cure themselves. Pushing on with rate rises into the spring of 2027, while crude heads for a glut, would not be prudence. It would be extreme incompetence.
